quotation: By a very early change Prim. Gmc. a > æ in OE and OFris. when not followed by a nasal consonant
paraphrase: Campbell gives the classic handbook statement of first fronting as an early OE and Frisian development with a nasal exception.
conditioning: Fronting applies when Germanic a is not followed by a nasal consonant.
chronology_claim: Treated as very early; later Campbell sections on breaking and restoration presuppose this fronted vowel as input.
exceptions_or_disagreements: Campbell also suggests the English and Frisian developments may have been independent rather than a single undifferentiated shared event.
terminology_used_by_source: early change; Prim. Gmc. a > æ
notes: Section-safe locator from the local text witness.

quotation: The restoration of a before a back vowel ... breaking can hardly be regarded otherwise than as a change affecting front vowels
paraphrase: Campbell explicitly derives later retraction and restoration from an earlier fronted stage, so fronting must precede both breaking and restoration.
conditioning: Breaking affects front vowels before consonant groups; restoration and retraction arise before following back vowels.
chronology_claim: Fronting precedes breaking, and restoration of a follows the breaking stage.
exceptions_or_disagreements: Dialect distribution varies, especially in Anglian and late West Saxon spellings.
terminology_used_by_source: breaking; retraction; restoration of a before back vowels
notes: Combined row because Campbell builds the relative chronology across these linked sections.

quotation: This vowel normally fronted to /ae/ by the sound change of Anglo-Frisian Brightening (or First Fronting).
paraphrase: Hogg supplies a concise modern formulation of the change and its standard label pair.
conditioning: Fronting is normal for short low a; following nasals block it.
chronology_claim: Placed among the very earliest stressed-syllable changes in pre-Old English.
exceptions_or_disagreements: Hogg emphasizes that later developments recreate back /a/ and complicate the synchronic OE vowel system.
notes: Page number is visible in the local OCR witness.

quotation: By First Fronting (see §3.3.4.1) / a / became /ae/ as in stressed syllables
paraphrase: Hogg extends first fronting into the unstressed-vowel system, which is useful support for the transducer's unstressed clause.
conditioning: Unstressed a fronts to æ; the resulting unstressed front vowels later merge toward e.
chronology_claim: Unstressed fronting precedes the later reduction and merger of unstressed front vowels.
exceptions_or_disagreements: Hogg marks the accompanying unstressed o > a step as only perhaps a chain shift.
notes: Useful specifically for the current FOMA unstressed clause.

quotation: Campbell offers a summary of traditional scholarly opinion ... (3) Fronting of West Gmc */a/ to /æ/ (4) Breaking and the related processes of retraction (5) Restoration of /a/ before back vowels
paraphrase: Toon reproduces Campbell's summary of traditional scholarly opinion on the ordering of the prehistoric changes (Campbell 1959: 109) and then argues that the list should not be read as a precise linear sequence.
conditioning: Fronting is treated separately from later breaking, retraction, and restoration.
chronology_claim: The row is most useful as a concise statement of the standard order fronting > breaking/retraction > restoration.
exceptions_or_disagreements: The exact sequencing of all prehistoric changes remains contested even if this local order is widely assumed.
notes: Chapter 6 of the Cambridge History volume edited by Hogg; the chapter is Toon's and is cited under its own key. OCR /ag/ normalized to /ae/ in the quotation for readability. Page verified against the chapter PDF: the list stands on p. 446, not p. 445.

quotation: Stressed low vowels were nasalized when immediately followed by a nasal in the northern WGmc dialects
paraphrase: Ringe and Taylor treat the nasal branch as the key exception to northern WGmc fronting and derive rounded outcomes like mona and comon from that path.
conditioning: Low vowels are nasalized before immediate nasals; non-nasal environments feed fronting instead.
chronology_claim: Treated as a shared northern WGmc development inherited by Old English rather than a late isolated OE innovation.
exceptions_or_disagreements: Rounding is presented as a later parallel development in diverging northern dialects rather than as the fronting event itself.
notes: Page-safe locator from the local text witness.

quotation: Since no specifically OE sound changes can be dated before the fronting, while one of the earliest must have followed it ... OE was already dialectally diverse when it became an identifiable dialect group.
paraphrase: Ringe and Taylor use dialect outcomes to argue that fronting is pre-breaking and already old enough to sit behind early OE dialect diversification.
conditioning: West Saxon keeps lower outcomes while Kentish, Mercian, and Northumbrian show higher reflexes.
chronology_claim: Fronting precedes breaking and belongs to the earliest recoverable OE prehistory.
exceptions_or_disagreements: They leave open whether much of the variable spread happened on the continent or in Britain.
notes: Good high-level chronology row for the dossier synthesis.

quotation: retraction must have occurred subsequently to fronting and subsequently to breaking
paraphrase: Ringe and Taylor make the cleanest explicit argument for the relative order fronting > breaking > general retraction.
conditioning: Retraction affects formerly fronted vowels before following back vowels after single consonants, geminates, or sC clusters.
chronology_claim: Retraction is later than both fronting and breaking.
exceptions_or_disagreements: The discussion is framed against the alternative view that some vowels were never fronted at all.
notes: This row is especially useful for chapter-order planning.

quotation: Elsewhere, a was fronted to æ ... This fronting is commonly referred to as Anglo-Frisian Brightening.
paraphrase: Fulk provides the clearest compact definition, examples, and terminology statement for the dossier pilot.
conditioning: Before nasal consonants a is nasalized and may later round; elsewhere it fronts to æ.
chronology_claim: Presented as an Anglo-Frisian development prior to the early Old English changes in the next section.
exceptions_or_disagreements: Fulk notes several Old Frisian environments where a remains unchanged, so the Anglo-Frisian picture is not fully uniform.
notes: Google Vision OCR witness used; the PDF was not needed for this row.

quotation: Before r plus any consonant ... æ and e are broken to ea and eo ... Before checked l the Anglian dialects show retraction rather than breaking of æ
paraphrase: Fulk's early OE section uses already-fronted æ as the input to breaking and records an Anglian retraction branch before checked l.
conditioning: Breaking targets front vowels before rC, lC, and h; Anglian checked-l contexts can retract rather than break.
chronology_claim: Breaking follows brightening and precedes later front-umlaut developments.
exceptions_or_disagreements: Dialectal retraction before checked l complicates any simple one-output account of the rule.
notes: This row links SC043 directly to its highest-priority order-sensitive neighbors.

quotation: Im Auslaut schwanden i und u unmittelbar nach langer Tonsilbe, und auch nach kurzer, wenn darauf noch eine andere Silbe folgte (nicht aber unmittelbar nach kurzer).
paraphrase: Luick states the core apocope rule as loss of final i and u after heavy syllables and after a short stressed syllable followed by another syllable.
conditioning: Final i and u are lost after long stressed syllables and in trisyllabic environments; they are retained immediately after a short stressed syllable.
chronology_claim: Treated as a specifically preliterary English development after i-umlaut.
exceptions_or_disagreements: Luick distinguishes this final loss from the separate medial developments discussed in later sections.
terminology_used_by_source: Urenglischer Schwund kurzer Vokale; i-, u-Schwund
notes: Local OCR/text witness; quotation lightly normalized for broken line wraps and spacing.

quotation: Überwog die letzte [Silbe] ... so schwand die Mittelsilbe: strengþu. Überwog die mittlere, so ... trat kein Schwund ein: heafodu ... Dieses Schwundgesetz, welches E. Sievers gefunden hat, ist sicher gemeinwestgermanisch
paraphrase: Luick is especially useful for the trisyllabic branch and for explicitly tying the law to Sievers.
conditioning: When both medial and final syllables are candidates, the outcome depends on prosodic weight relations; forms like strengþu and heafodu split accordingly.
chronology_claim: The i/u-loss follows i-umlaut and precedes later prehistoric developments such as vowel-expansion processes discussed immediately afterward.
exceptions_or_disagreements: The alternating trisyllabic outcomes show why the rule cannot be reduced to a naive final-position deletion.
notes: Local OCR/text witness; quotation lightly normalized for broken line wraps and spacing.

quotation: w and ȳ ... were lost in Prim. OE, in final unaccented syllables after a long accented syllable, or a short accented syllable and another syllable. They remained after a short accented syllable, or a long accented syllable followed by a short syllable.
paraphrase: Campbell gives the classic handbook formulation of OE high-vowel apocope in terms of syllable weight and trisyllabic structure.
conditioning: Final high vowels are lost after heavy monosyllables and after short stressed syllables followed by another syllable; they remain after simple light monosyllables and after long stressed syllables followed by a short syllable.
chronology_claim: Placed in the early OE loss of unaccented vowels after the preceding medial-vowel syncopation sections.
exceptions_or_disagreements: Campbell's notation uses older vowel symbols, but the conditioning matches the live rule closely.
terminology_used_by_source: early Old English loss; final unaccented syllables
notes: Section-safe locator from the local text witness; no substantive normalization.

quotation: When i and u of a final syllable are followed by a consonant, there is no loss ... The weight of the second element seems to have had influence upon the loss of medial vowels in compounds
paraphrase: Campbell sharpens the rule by separating pure final apocope from environments where a following consonant blocks loss and by tracking weight effects in compounds.
conditioning: No loss occurs when the final high vowel is followed by a consonant; compound structure and the weight of the following element can affect medial-vowel loss.
chronology_claim: These sections situate apocope within a broader early OE weak-tail and syncopation complex.
exceptions_or_disagreements: The compound evidence shows why some apparent counterexamples are really different structural contexts.
terminology_used_by_source: syncopation; compounds; final syllable blocked by following consonant
notes: Useful for matching the transducer's interaction with later weak-tail cleanup.

quotation: Apocope affected the high vowels /i/ and /u/ and occurred most regularly when they were preceded by a single heavy syllable ... But apocope also occurred in trisyllabic words if the first syllable was light
paraphrase: Hogg gives the cleanest compact modern summary of the rule and its main trisyllabic extension.
conditioning: The targeted vowels are final i and u; the main conditioning is heavy monosyllables plus a special trisyllabic pattern where the first syllable is light.
chronology_claim: Hogg treats vowel loss as earlier than the later reduction in the variety of unstressed vowels.
exceptions_or_disagreements: Hogg immediately contrasts forms like weorod and heafodu, which is useful for dossier-level counterexample control.
notes: Page number is visible in the local text witness.

quotation: The high vowels were also subject to syncope in medial positions after a heavy syllable
paraphrase: Hogg explicitly pairs apocope with medial syncope, making the dossier's order-sensitivity framing easier to explain.
conditioning: Medial i/u syncope follows heavy syllables, while final apocope targets word-final high vowels.
chronology_claim: Syncope is discussed as part of the same early loss of unstressed vowels but as a distinct process from apocope.
exceptions_or_disagreements: The pairing explains why some paradigms can look as though one rule or the other has overapplied.
notes: Page-safe locator from the local text witness.

quotation: After general syncope had run its course, short *i and *u were lost word-finally after a heavy syllable and after an unstressed syllable preceded by a stressed light syllable.
paraphrase: Ringe and Taylor provide the clearest explicit ordering of apocope after general syncope and a precise statement of the two main conditioning environments.
conditioning: Final short i/u are lost after heavy syllables and after trisyllabic sequences with stressed light + unstressed + final vowel.
chronology_claim: Apocope follows general syncope.
exceptions_or_disagreements: Their section is morphologically organized, so the examples are abundant but dispersed across paradigms.

quotation: Apocope and the shortening of unstressed long vowels are the last prehistoric OE sound changes
paraphrase: Ringe and Taylor give the strongest concise chronology statement for placing SC063 at the end of prehistoric OE.

chronology_claim: Apocope is one of the last prehistoric OE sound changes.

quotation: the pattern of retention of unstressed high vowels after light syllables but not heavy is plainer in WGmc. than elsewhere
paraphrase: Fulk gives a compact comparative statement of the heavy-vs-light split and then illustrates it with OE examples.
conditioning: Unstressed high vowels are retained after light syllables but not after heavy ones.
chronology_claim: Fulk treats the change as part of later preliterary changes of medial and final vowels.
exceptions_or_disagreements: He emphasizes that OS and OHG obscure the original pattern more than OE through analogy.
